title: Where humans came from: many kinds of humans, and what old bones and DNA tell us

summary.text: Today there is only one kind of human on Earth. A hundred thousand years ago there were at least five, and they lived at the same time. Where did the others go? In this lesson you will feel four clues on your own skull, and follow one ancestor's DNA down the generations with squared paper, a coin and number chits. You will see why most people alive today carry small pieces of Neanderthal DNA, and why your pieces differ from your neighbour's. You will also weigh a question that scientists still argue about: what, if anything, makes our kind different?
summary.art: A girl at a table colouring rows of squares red and white, with a coin and a cup of paper chits beside her, and behind her five faint outlines of different human heads in a row.

intro.hook: If you had walked across Asia 100,000 years ago, you could have met at least five different kinds of humans. Today you would meet only one kind, us. What happened to the other four?
intro.text: For a long time the answer seemed simple: they died out, and nothing of them was left. Then scientists learned to read DNA from bones tens of thousands of years old. The DNA showed something nobody could have seen in the bones alone. Our ancestors met some of these other humans and had children with them, and pieces of their DNA are still inside most people alive today. In this lesson you will find out who the other humans were, how a bone or a speck of bone powder can tell us about them, and what is still unknown. India has a part in this story too, and a big gap in it.
intro.art: A map of Africa, Europe and Asia with five small figures of different heights and builds standing in different regions, and a child of today looking at them from the corner.

outcomes: By the end I can name at least four other kinds of humans, say where and when they lived, and explain that several kinds lived at the same time.
By the end I can say what a fossil bone or tooth can tell us about a person, and what it cannot.
By the end I can explain how scientists read DNA from old bones, and why heat, time and contamination make it hard.
By the end I can use my results from the Shrinking Pieces Test to explain why each person carries only small, different pieces of Neanderthal DNA.
By the end I can explain how DNA showed that different kinds of humans had children together.
By the end I can give two ideas about what makes our kind of human different, with evidence for and against each.
By the end I can say which parts of the human story are known, which are argued about, and what nobody knows yet.

terms.meaning: Homo sapiens is the scientific name of our own kind of human. Every person alive today is Homo sapiens.
terms.example: The oldest known fossils on our line come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco. They are about 315,000 years old.
terms.art: A group of people of many ages and skin colours standing together, all labelled with the same name.

terms.meaning: Neanderthals were a kind of human who lived in Europe and western and central Asia. They were gone as a separate people by about 40,000 years ago.
terms.example: A Neanderthal had a long, low skull, a thick ridge of bone over the eyes and no chin. Their brain was as big as ours.
terms.art: A strongly built woman with a heavy brow ridge and a broad nose, wearing an animal skin and tending a fire in a cave mouth.

terms.meaning: Denisovans were a kind of human who lived in Asia. They were first recognised from the DNA in one finger bone, not from the shape of any bone.
terms.example: The finger bone was found in 2008 in Denisova Cave in Siberia. That cave gave the Denisovans their name.
terms.art: A tiny finger bone on a gloved palm, with a cave opening in a snowy mountain behind.

terms.meaning: A species is one kind of living being. One common test is that members of a species can have young together, and those young can have young too.
terms.example: Tigers are one species and lions are another. The test does not always give a clear answer, as the Neanderthals show.
terms.art: A tiger and a lion side by side with a dotted line drawn between them and a question mark on the line.

terms.meaning: A fossil is a remain or a trace of a living being from long ago, kept in rock or soil. A bone, a tooth and a footprint can all be fossils.
terms.example: The Narmada skull, found at Hathnora in Madhya Pradesh in 1982, is a fossil of an ancient human.
terms.art: The top of a brown skull half buried in gravel on a river bank.

terms.meaning: DNA is the long molecule in every cell that carries the instructions for building and running a body. The instructions are written in four chemical letters: A, T, C and G.
terms.example: Your DNA has about 3 billion letters. You got one set from your mother and one set from your father.
terms.art: A twisted ladder with coloured rungs, and a long line of the letters A, T, C and G running out of it.

terms.meaning: A genome is the complete set of DNA instructions of one living being.
terms.example: The first rough copy of a Neanderthal genome was read in 2010 from three bones found in Vindija Cave in Croatia.
terms.art: A thick book whose pages are filled with rows of the letters A, T, C and G.

terms.meaning: Ancient DNA is DNA taken from the remains of a being who died long ago. It is broken into very short pieces and mixed with the DNA of microbes.
terms.example: The oldest DNA read from any human relative comes from bones in a Spanish cave. They are about 430,000 years old.
terms.art: A scientist in a white suit, hood and mask drilling a tiny hole in an old bone inside a clean room.

terms.meaning: A chromosome is one long thread of DNA. Human cells have 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. One of each pair came from the mother and one from the father.
terms.example: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, each row of 20 squares stands for one chromosome.
terms.art: Twenty-three pairs of small X-shaped threads laid out in rows.

terms.meaning: Crossing over happens when a body makes an egg cell or a sperm cell. The two chromosomes of a pair swap parts, so the child gets a chromosome that is part one grandparent's and part the other's.
terms.example: Because of crossing over, a long piece of an ancestor's DNA is cut shorter in each generation.
terms.art: Two long strips, one red and one white, crossing each other and coming apart as two strips that are each part red and part white.

terms.meaning: Mitochondrial DNA is a small separate loop of DNA in the mitochondria, the parts of a cell that release energy. A child gets it only from the mother.
terms.example: Denny's mitochondrial DNA was the Neanderthal kind. That told scientists that her mother was a Neanderthal.
terms.art: A cell with several bean-shaped mitochondria, each holding a small ring of DNA, and an arrow from a mother to a child.

terms.meaning: Interbreeding means that members of two different groups have children together.
terms.example: About 47,000 years ago, our ancestors and Neanderthals interbred. Their children were part of our ancestors' families.
terms.art: Two families of slightly different build sitting around one fire, with a small child between them.

terms.meaning: Contamination means that something from outside has got into a sample. In ancient DNA work, it means DNA from microbes or from living people has got mixed in.
terms.example: A person who picks up an old bone with bare hands leaves skin cells on the bone. Those cells carry today's human DNA.
terms.art: A bare thumb pressing on an old bone, leaving a glowing fingerprint made of tiny letters.

terms.meaning: Collagen is the main protein in bone. Proteins are long chains built by cells, and they last longer in old bones than DNA does.
terms.example: The collagen of a human bone differs a little from the collagen of a hyena bone. A machine can tell them apart from a tiny chip.
terms.art: A bone cut across to show fibres inside, with one fibre drawn large as a twisted rope.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being is extinct when no members are left alive.
terms.example: Homo floresiensis, a small human from the island of Flores in Indonesia, is extinct. No one has found their DNA in living people.
terms.art: An empty cave with small stone tools left on the floor.

terms.meaning: A hybrid is a child whose parents came from two different kinds or groups.
terms.example: Denny, who lived about 90,000 years ago, had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
terms.art: A girl standing between a mother and a father who look a little different from each other.

terms.meaning: Cumulative culture means that each generation learns what the last one knew and then adds to it. Skills build up over time.
terms.example: Nobody could invent a bicycle alone from nothing. The wheel, the chain and the rubber tyre were each worked out by different people long ago.
terms.art: A row of people passing an object along, where the object changes from a sharp stone to a knife to a pair of scissors.

explanations.concept: Several kinds of humans lived at the same time
explanations.definition: For most of the last 300,000 years, our species shared the Earth with other kinds of humans. We have been the only kind for only the last 40,000 years or so.
explanations.description: People often draw human evolution as one line: an ape, then a bent figure, then an upright one, then us. That picture is wrong. The human family was a branching bush, and many branches were alive at once. Our own species, Homo sapiens, began in Africa. The oldest known fossils on our line are about 315,000 years old. At that time Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans lived further east. A small-brained human called Homo naledi lived in southern Africa. On the island of Java, Homo erectus lived on until about 110,000 years ago. On two other islands lived two very small kinds of humans, Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis. Why does this matter? Because it changes the question. We should not ask how one line led to us. We should ask why, out of so many kinds, only one is left. Nobody has a full answer yet.
examples: About 100,000 years ago there were at least five kinds: Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis.
The last Homo erectus known, from Ngandong in Java, lived between 117,000 and 108,000 years ago.
In the activity Who Lived When, you draw each kind as a bar on a time line and count how many bars overlap.
explanations.art: A bushy tree with many branches, most ending in a small cross, several branches running side by side at the same height, and one branch reaching the top.

explanations.definition: Neanderthals were a kind of human who lived across Europe and as far east as Siberia. They made fire and tools, cared for their injured, and were gone as a separate people by about 40,000 years ago.
explanations.description: The first Neanderthal bones to be recognised were found in 1856 in the Neander Valley in Germany. A schoolteacher, Johann Carl Fuhlrott, saw that they were not from a person of today. A Neanderthal skull is long and low, with a thick ridge of bone over the eyes and a bulge at the back. The jaw has no chin. The body was short, broad and very strong. For many years people pictured Neanderthals as dull brutes. The evidence does not support that picture. Their brains were as big as ours, and on average a little bigger. They made fine stone tools, kept fires and probably wore coverings of animal skin. Most scientists accept that they buried at least some of their dead. One man from Shanidar Cave in Iraq had a crushed eye socket, a withered right arm and damaged legs. His bones show that he lived for years after these injuries. The scientists who studied him think he could not have done that alone. Other Neanderthals must have fed and protected him. Why were they gone by 40,000 years ago? Scientists have several ideas, and you will meet them in another card.
examples: Neanderthal skulls held brains of about 1,460 to 1,640 cubic centimetres. Brains of people today are about 1,300 cubic centimetres on average.
The Shanidar man lived with a useless arm and one damaged eye. His injuries had healed, so they happened long before he died.
Red marks in three Spanish caves were dated to more than 64,000 years ago and credited to Neanderthals. Other scientists doubt the dating.
explanations.art: A Neanderthal family in a cave mouth in snowy country: a woman scraping a hide with a stone tool, a child watching, and an older man with one arm held close to his chest sitting by the fire.

explanations.concept: Denisovans: a people first known from DNA
explanations.definition: Denisovans were a kind of human who lived in Asia. Scientists found out that they existed by reading the DNA in a finger bone, before anyone knew what a Denisovan looked like.
explanations.description: In 2008, Russian archaeologists found a small piece of a girl's finger bone in Denisova Cave, in the Altai Mountains of Siberia. Nobody could tell from the shape whose it was. In 2010 Svante Pääbo's team in Leipzig, Germany, read the DNA. The DNA was not that of our species, and not Neanderthal. The girl belonged to a group nobody had known about. This was the first time a kind of human was discovered from DNA alone. For years the only Denisovan remains were that finger bone and a few teeth. Then other fossils were matched to them, mostly by proteins. Proteins last longer than DNA. A jaw from a cave about 3,300 metres up on the Tibetan Plateau was matched in 2019. A jaw dredged from the sea floor near Taiwan was matched in 2025. In the same year a nearly complete skull from Harbin in China was matched too, using proteins and DNA from the hardened plaque on a tooth. So Denisovans finally have a face: a large, long skull with a heavy brow ridge. They lived from cold Siberia to the high plateau and probably far into Southeast Asia. Scientists have still not agreed on a species name for them.
examples: The Xiahe jaw from the Tibetan Plateau is at least 160,000 years old. A monk found it in 1980, and nobody knew what it was for almost 40 years.
Many Tibetan people carry a version of a gene called EPAS1 that helps the body cope with thin mountain air. The version came from Denisovans.
The Ayta Magbukon people of the Philippines carry about 5 percent Denisovan DNA, the highest share known.
explanations.art: A cave in a snowy mountainside, and beside it three small objects drawn large: a finger bone, a big molar tooth and a jaw bone, each with a line to a row of DNA letters.

explanations.concept: The small humans of the islands, and Homo naledi
explanations.definition: Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis were very small humans who lived on islands in Southeast Asia. Homo naledi was a small-brained human from southern Africa. Where each came from is still argued about.
explanations.description: In 2003, a team led by Thomas Sutikna and Mike Morwood dug up a skeleton in Liang Bua cave on the island of Flores in Indonesia. She was an adult woman only about 1.06 metres tall, with a brain about the size of a chimpanzee's. Her kind was named Homo floresiensis. They made stone tools and lived on Flores until about 50,000 years ago. How did they come to be so small? Most scientists think their ancestors were larger humans who reached the island more than 700,000 years ago. On small islands with little food, large animals often become smaller over many generations, because a small body needs less food. Some scientists think instead that they came from an older, smaller kind of human. In 2019 another small human, Homo luzonensis, was named from Callao Cave on Luzon in the Philippines. Homo naledi was found in 2013 deep inside the Rising Star cave in South Africa. Six women scientists who could squeeze through the narrow passage brought out more than 1,550 pieces of bone. Homo naledi had a brain less than half the size of ours and lived only about 300,000 years ago. So big brains were not the only way to be human at that time.
examples: The elephant relatives called Stegodon also became small on Flores. Island life changed them and the humans in the same direction.
Homo luzonensis had small teeth and curved finger and toe bones. At least three individuals are known.
Lee Berger's team says Homo naledi buried their dead in the cave. Most other scientists who reviewed the evidence were not convinced.
explanations.art: A woman of today standing beside a Homo floresiensis woman who reaches only to her waist, with a small elephant-like Stegodon in the background.

explanations.concept: What a fossil can tell us, and what it cannot
explanations.definition: A fossil bone or tooth can show a person's size, age, injuries and way of moving. It cannot show their skin, hair, words or thoughts.
explanations.description: A fossil is a small part of a body, and scientists read it closely. The length of a thigh bone gives the height. Teeth show the age, because teeth grow in a fixed order and lay down thin growth lines. Healed breaks show injuries that the person lived through. The shape of the hip and the place where the spine joins the skull show how the person walked. But soft parts rot, so a fossil is silent about skin, hair, voice and thoughts. Fossils are also very rare. A body becomes a fossil only if it is buried quickly and the minerals in the ground are right. This is where India's gap comes in. India has stone tools that are more than a million years old. Those at Attirampakkam near Chennai, studied by Shanti Pappu and Kumar Akhilesh, are about 1.5 million years old. So ancient humans certainly lived here. Yet almost none of their bones have been found. The main one is the Narmada skull, found by the geologist Arun Sonakia on 5 December 1982. She was probably a woman in her thirties. Scientists still argue about how long ago she lived and about which kind of human she was. No DNA has been read from her, so that question stays open.
examples: Feel your own chin. A chin that sticks out is found only in our species, so a jaw with a chin tells scientists the jaw is Homo sapiens.
Scratches on teeth and chemicals in bone show what a person ate. Neanderthals in cold places ate a lot of meat.
The tool makers of Attirampakkam left thousands of hand axes. Nobody knows which kind of human they were, because no bones were found with the tools.
explanations.art: A skeleton laid out on a table with labels pointing to a thigh bone 'height', teeth 'age and food', a healed rib 'old injury', and empty question marks floating where skin, hair and voice would be.

explanations.concept: How DNA is read from old bones
explanations.definition: After death, DNA breaks into short pieces and slowly falls apart. Scientists collect the short pieces from bone powder, read them, and fit them together by where they overlap.
explanations.description: In a living cell, each chromosome is one unbroken thread of DNA, millions of letters long. Living cells repair their DNA all the time. After death the repair stops. Water reacts with the DNA and cuts the thread, again and again. After thousands of years the pieces are often shorter than 50 letters. Why do cold places matter? These cutting reactions are chemical reactions, and chemical reactions go faster when it is warm. So DNA lasts longest in cold, dry caves and frozen ground. That is one reason the richest finds come from Siberia and Europe, and why no ancient human DNA has yet been read from India's oldest fossils. There is a second problem. Most of the DNA in an old bone is not from the person. It comes from microbes that lived in the bone after death, and from every person who touched the bone. So the work is done in clean rooms, by people in suits, masks and gloves. The pieces are read by machines. A computer then lines them up against a known human genome and uses overlaps to put them in order. Each place is read many times, so that one damaged piece cannot mislead. Where no DNA is left, proteins such as collagen can still help, because they last longer.
examples: In the activity The Shredded Message, you rebuild a sentence from short overlapping pieces, with pieces of a different sentence mixed in.
In the activity Warm or Cold, the same powder fizzes away faster in warm water than in cold. DNA also breaks down faster in warmth.
The oldest DNA from a human relative is about 430,000 years old. It comes from a cave in Spain called Sima de los Huesos.
explanations.art: Three panels: a long unbroken ribbon of letters in a living cell, the same ribbon cut into many short scraps in an old bone, and a computer screen lining the scraps up in overlapping rows.

explanations.concept: What the old DNA showed: the kinds of humans mixed
explanations.definition: DNA from old bones shows that our ancestors had children with Neanderthals and with Denisovans, and that Neanderthals and Denisovans had children with each other.
explanations.description: In 2010, Pääbo's team compared the Neanderthal genome with the genomes of people living today. People whose ancestors lived outside Africa shared a little more DNA with Neanderthals than people from Africa south of the Sahara did. The best explanation is that Neanderthals and our ancestors had children together after some of our ancestors left Africa. Today about 2 percent of the DNA of people outside Africa came from Neanderthals. Later studies found that people across Africa also carry a little, about 0.3 percent. It was probably carried back by people who returned to Africa. Denisovan DNA is found too. It makes up about 5 percent in some peoples of the Philippines, New Guinea and Australia, and a small trace across South and East Asia. A study of 2,762 people in India, published in 2025, found that 1 to 2 percent of their DNA came from Neanderthals and Denisovans. The clearest proof of mixing is a girl nicknamed Denny, who lived about 90,000 years ago. Half of her DNA was Neanderthal and half was Denisovan. Her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan. Why is this certain? At place after place in her DNA, one copy was the Neanderthal kind and the other was the Denisovan kind. That pattern appears only in a child of the first generation.
examples: A man who lived about 40,000 years ago in what is now Romania had 6 to 9 percent Neanderthal DNA. He had a Neanderthal ancestor only four to six generations before him.
Any two people today are about 99.9 percent the same in their DNA. A person today and a Neanderthal are about 99.7 percent the same.
In the activity Whose Child, you read pairs of DNA markers to work out who a mystery child's parents were.
explanations.art: A simple family tree with three coloured branches labelled 'our ancestors', 'Neanderthals' and 'Denisovans', and thin arrows crossing between the branches where children were born.

explanations.concept: Why the Neanderthal pieces are short, and different in each person
explanations.definition: Crossing over cuts an ancestor's DNA into shorter pieces in every generation, and chance decides which pieces are passed on. So each person keeps only a few small pieces, and different people keep different ones.
explanations.description: Think back to the Shrinking Pieces Test. The first child had a whole red chromosome from the red ancestor. In each new generation, crossing over swapped part of that chromosome for a white part. The red piece got shorter, and in many family lines the red was lost completely. But different lines kept different pieces. The same has happened to Neanderthal DNA for about 47,000 years. That is why no person today has a whole Neanderthal chromosome. Each person outside Africa has thousands of short pieces, adding up to about 2 percent. Your pieces are not the same as your neighbour's. When scientists add up the different pieces carried by many people, a large part of a Neanderthal genome appears. A study of people in Iceland recovered about 41 percent. The 2025 study in India recovered about half. The length of the pieces is also a clock. Long pieces mean the mixing was recent, and short pieces mean it was long ago. That is how scientists worked out that most of the mixing happened about 47,000 years ago, over about 7,000 years. The paper test is simplified in one way. In the test the share halved every generation, because every partner was all white. In real life, after the mixing, nearly everyone in the group carried some pieces. So the share stopped falling quickly and stayed near 2 percent, while the pieces kept getting shorter.
examples: Some Neanderthal pieces helped. Several affect how the body fights germs, and they became common.
Some pieces seem to have done harm and were lost. Long stretches of our DNA, including much of the X chromosome, have almost no Neanderthal pieces.
The man from Romania had very long Neanderthal pieces. That is how scientists knew his Neanderthal ancestor lived only a few generations before him.
explanations.art: Five rows of squares one under another, the top row all red, each lower row with a shorter red block, and beside them six people each holding a different small red piece.

explanations.definition: Scientists do not agree on whether Neanderthals and our ancestors were two species or two groups within one species.
explanations.description: A common test of a species is that members can have children together, and those children can have children too. Neanderthals and our ancestors did that, and so did Denisovans. By that test, all three were one species. Yet their skulls and bodies were clearly different, and the groups had lived apart for more than 500,000 years. There is also a sign that the mixing did not always go well, because some parts of our DNA hold almost no Neanderthal pieces. Why can't the question be settled? Because a species is a way of sorting that people made. Living beings change slowly, and two groups that are drifting apart pass through a long time when they are neither fully one nor fully two. Neanderthals and our ancestors met during that in-between time.
examples: Lions and tigers can have cubs together in zoos, yet everyone counts them as two species.
Some scientists write Homo neanderthalensis, a separate species. Others write Homo sapiens neanderthalensis, a group within our species.
Denisovans have no agreed scientific name at all.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the shapes of bones, such as Ian Tattersall and Chris Stringer
perspectives.explanation: Neanderthals were a separate species, Homo neanderthalensis. Their skulls and skeletons differ from ours as clearly as those of other close species. A little mixing does not erase that.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use the test of having children together
perspectives.explanation: Neanderthals, Denisovans and our ancestors had healthy children whose descendants are alive today. So they were groups within one species.

perspectives.who: Svante Pääbo, who read the Neanderthal genome
perspectives.explanation: The argument cannot be settled, because there is no single definition of a species that fits every case. It is more useful to describe what happened than to argue about the label.

explanations.art: Two skulls side by side, one tall and round with a chin and one long and low with a brow ridge, with a dotted line between them that fades out halfway down.

explanations.definition: There is no agreed answer to what sets our kind of human apart. Almost every ability once called 'only human' has been found in other humans or in other animals.
explanations.description: People have offered many answers: making tools, using fire, speaking, making art, burying the dead, caring for the weak. The evidence has taken away most of them. Chimpanzees and crows make tools. Neanderthals used fire, made glue from birch bark and cared for injured friends. So scientists now look for differences of amount, not of kind. One strong idea is cumulative culture. We teach, the learner improves the skill a little, and teaches it again. In a real experiment in 2015, Thomas Morgan and his team asked 184 people to learn to make simple stone tools. Some could only look at finished tools. Some could watch a maker. Some were taught with words. The skill passed along a chain of learners well only when there was teaching, and best of all with words. Another idea is that our ancestors lived in larger groups and kept in touch with friends far away, so good ideas were not lost. A third idea looks at DNA. A small number of DNA changes are shared by nearly everyone today and missing in Neanderthals and Denisovans. Scientists are testing what those changes do. Nobody knows yet whether any of them matters much. The honest answer is that we differ from other humans and other animals in degree, and nobody knows whether any single thing explains it.
examples: In the Teaching Test, you compare how well a paper fold is learned by watching alone and by watching with words.
Neanderthals carried the same version of FOXP2, a gene needed for speech, as people today. Whether they spoke as we do is not known.
The one clear feature of the skeleton that only our species has is the chin. Nobody is sure what the chin is for.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, in The Descent of Man (1871)
perspectives.explanation: The difference in mind between humans and other animals is great, but it is a difference of degree and not of kind.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study culture, such as Kevin Laland and Thomas Morgan
perspectives.explanation: What sets us apart is teaching and language working together. They let skills build up over generations until no one person could invent them alone.

perspectives.who: Scientists who stress symbols, such as Ian Tattersall
perspectives.explanation: Our species thinks in symbols, such as words, pictures and numbers. This way of thinking is new and special to us, and it appeared late and quite suddenly.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study Neanderthal sites, such as Francesco d'Errico and João Zilhão
perspectives.explanation: Neanderthals used colours and ornaments and may have made marks on cave walls. Symbols were not ours alone.

explanations.art: A circle of small pictures, a stone tool, a fire, a painted hand, a grave with flowers and two people talking, each with a small label showing which other humans or animals also do it.

explanations.concept: Why are we the only humans left?
explanations.definition: Nobody knows for certain why the other kinds of humans disappeared. The main ideas are changing climate, small numbers, competition with our ancestors, and being absorbed by mixing.
explanations.description: Neanderthals had lived through many ice ages before our ancestors arrived in Europe. Within about ten thousand years of that arrival, they were gone as a separate people. What happened? The first thing to know is that there were never many Neanderthals. Their DNA shows little variety, which means their groups were small and thinly spread. A small group can die out by bad luck alone: a few hard winters, a sickness, too few babies. Our ancestors came in larger numbers. They may have taken the best hunting grounds without any fighting. The climate was also swinging between cold and mild at that time. And some Neanderthals joined our ancestors' families, so part of their people was absorbed. Most scientists think several of these causes worked together. For the Denisovans and the small island humans, there is even less evidence.
examples: Studies of Neanderthal DNA suggest only a few thousand breeding adults at a time across all of Europe and western Asia.
Homo floresiensis disappears from Liang Bua about 50,000 years ago, close to when our species reached that region. Nobody knows whether the two met.
Toss 4 coins, and all 4 land tails about once in 16 tries. A group of four families can have that kind of bad luck. A group of four hundred almost never does.

perspectives.who: Scientists who stress numbers, such as Krist Vaesen
perspectives.explanation: Neanderthal groups were so small that chance, with no help from us, could have ended them.

perspectives.who: Scientists who stress competition, such as Chris Stringer
perspectives.explanation: Our ancestors arrived in larger, better connected groups and slowly took over the food and the land.
Neanderthals did not only die out. Many were absorbed into our ancestors' much larger population, and their DNA lives on.

explanations.art: A wide snowy valley with one small Neanderthal camp fire in the distance and a larger group of newcomers walking in from the other side.

agreed.text: Our species, Homo sapiens, began in Africa.
agreed.evidence: The oldest fossils on our line are African, such as those from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years old. People in Africa also have the most variety in their DNA, which is what an oldest home looks like.

agreed.text: Several kinds of humans lived at the same time as our species.
agreed.evidence: Dated fossils of Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo naledi, Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and late Homo erectus all fall within the last 335,000 years.

agreed.text: Our ancestors had children with Neanderthals and with Denisovans.
agreed.evidence: Genomes read from old bones match short pieces of DNA carried by living people. People outside Africa carry about 2 percent Neanderthal DNA.

agreed.text: Neanderthals and Denisovans had children with each other.
agreed.evidence: The genome of Denny, read in 2018 from a bone 2.5 centimetres long, is half Neanderthal and half Denisovan.

agreed.text: All people alive today are one species, and very alike.
agreed.evidence: Any two people differ in about one DNA letter in a thousand. That is less variety than is found within chimpanzees.

agreed.text: DNA breaks down with time, and faster in warm places.
agreed.evidence: The oldest genomes come from frozen ground and cold caves. Very little old DNA has been recovered from hot, wet regions.

challenging.who: Marcellin Boule, a French scientist, who described a Neanderthal skeleton from 1908 onwards
challenging.for: The skeleton he studied was bent, and the heavy brow and jaw looked rough to people of his time.
challenging.against: The man had been old and ill, which bent his bones. Neanderthals stood as upright as we do, had large brains, made fire and tools, and cared for their injured.
challenging.context: This card is about an old picture of Neanderthals that is still common in cartoons.

challenging.claim: Neanderthals died out without leaving any descendants.
challenging.who: Many scientists before 2010, after the first small piece of Neanderthal DNA was read in 1997
challenging.for: The first DNA read was mitochondrial DNA, and no living person has the Neanderthal kind.
challenging.against: The whole genome, read in 2010, showed Neanderthal pieces in people outside Africa. Mitochondrial DNA is one tiny part, passed on only by mothers, and can be lost by chance.
challenging.context: This card is about what scientists thought before whole genomes could be read from old bones.

challenging.who: Dirk Hoffmann, Alistair Pike and others, in 2018
challenging.for: Thin mineral crusts over red marks in three Spanish caves were dated to more than 64,000 years. That is before our species is known to have reached Spain.
challenging.against: Other scientists say the crust that was dated may not lie directly over the paint, so the paint could be much younger.
challenging.context: This card is about whether making marks and pictures belonged only to our species.

challenging.claim: Homo naledi buried their dead and scratched marks on the cave wall.
challenging.who: Lee Berger and his team, in 2023
challenging.for: Bodies lay in hollows deep in a cave that is very hard to reach, and there are crossed lines on a wall nearby.
challenging.against: The scientists who reviewed the reports said the evidence did not show that the hollows were dug or that the marks were made by Homo naledi.
challenging.context: This card is about a claim that a small-brained human did things once thought to need a big brain.

challenging.claim: Modern humans arose in many regions at once, from the older humans living in each region.
challenging.who: Milford Wolpoff, Alan Thorne and Wu Xinzhi, from 1984
challenging.for: Some features of old skulls in Asia look a little like those of people living there now.
challenging.against: DNA shows that almost all the ancestry of every living person goes back to Africa within the last 300,000 years. Older regional humans added only a few percent.
challenging.context: This card is about an older idea of where people today came from. It was partly right about mixing and wrong about the main story.

big_questions.q: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, a line that lost every red square still had the red ancestor in the family. Are you descended from someone whose DNA you do not carry?
big_questions.hint: Count your ancestors ten generations back. Then think about how many pieces your DNA could be cut into.

big_questions.q: Neanderthals are called extinct. Yet together, living people carry about half of a Neanderthal genome. Are Neanderthals gone?
big_questions.hint: Decide first what you mean by 'gone'. Is a people their bodies, their way of life, or their DNA?

big_questions.q: If Neanderthals were alive today, would they go to school with you? What would be fair?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you would need to know about them first, and who should decide.

big_questions.q: Almost everything once called 'only human' has been found in another kind of human or another animal. Does our kind need to be special?
big_questions.hint: Ask why people want a clear line. Then ask what would change if there were none.

big_questions.q: Scientists knew Denisovans existed before they knew what a Denisovan looked like. What does it mean to 'know' a people?
big_questions.hint: Compare what DNA tells, what a skull tells, and what neither can tell.

big_questions.q: India has tools a million years old and almost no bones. How sure can we be about a story when most of the evidence is missing?
big_questions.hint: Think of a jigsaw with most pieces lost. What can you still say, and what must you leave open?

story.title: One Bone in Two Thousand
story.note: This is a true story. The cave, the dates, the people, the number of bone pieces, the collagen test, the result and the checks are all real. Viviane Slon has said that her first thought was that she had made a mistake, and Svante Pääbo has said he first thought the laboratory had slipped up. The order in which the bone pieces were tested is not known, so the count before the find is imagined. What Samantha Brown and Viviane Slon were thinking and feeling while they worked is imagined, and so are the words in quotation marks.
text: In 2012, archaeologists digging in Denisova Cave, in the mountains of Siberia, lifted a splinter of bone out of the earth. It was about as long as the top joint of your thumb. It had no shape that anyone could name. It went into a bag with other splinters like it.

The cave had given up thousands of such splinters. Most were bits of animals that had lived and died around the cave. A few, perhaps, were human. But a splinter of a deer and a splinter of a person look the same to the eye. So the bags were labelled 'unidentifiable' and put away.

In 2015, some of those bags travelled to the University of Oxford in England. Two scientists there, Katerina Douka and Tom Higham, had a plan. A student named Samantha Brown took it on as the project for her master's degree.

The plan used collagen, the main protein in bone. Collagen is a long chain, and the chain is a little different in each kind of animal. A machine can weigh the broken bits of the chain very exactly. The pattern of weights works like a fingerprint. A hyena gives one pattern, a horse gives another, and a human gives a third.

So Samantha could find a human bone without knowing its shape. She only had to take a tiny chip from every splinter, treat it, and send it through the machine at the University of Manchester. There were 2,315 splinters.
She began. Chip, label, test. The first pattern was an animal. So was the second. So was the hundredth.

Weeks went by. Five hundred splinters. A thousand. Every one an animal. A project like this can end with nothing at all, and a student has only so much time. 'Maybe there is no human in these bags,' she thought. She picked up the next splinter anyway.

Then one pattern was different. It was the pattern of the human family. The splinter was number DC1227. It was 2.5 centimetres long and weighed less than two grams. It was the only human bone among the 2,315.
The collagen test could say 'human'. It could not say which kind of human. For that, the splinter had to go to Leipzig in Germany, to the laboratory that had read the first Neanderthal genome.

There the scientists drilled out a little bone powder in a clean room. First they read the mitochondrial DNA. This is the small loop of DNA that a child gets only from the mother. It was the Neanderthal kind. So the bone seemed to belong to a Neanderthal.

A young scientist named Viviane Slon went on to read the rest of the DNA, the part that comes from both parents. The result made no sense. About half of the pieces matched Neanderthals. The other half matched Denisovans, the people known from a finger bone in the same cave.

Viviane's first thought was not 'what a discovery'. It was 'what did I do wrong?' Had powder from two bones been mixed? Had something got into the sample? In this kind of work, a strange result is usually a mistake.
So she tested the result before she trusted it. She took bone powder again, six samples in all, and prepared each one separately. All six gave the same answer: half and half.

Then she looked at how the two halves were arranged. Remember that a child has two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. If this person's family had been mixed long ago, the two kinds of DNA would lie in patches. Some places would have two Neanderthal copies, and some would have two Denisovan copies.

That was not the pattern. At place after place, all along the chromosomes, there was one Neanderthal copy and one Denisovan copy. Only one kind of family gives that pattern. One parent was a Neanderthal, and the other parent was a Denisovan.
The mitochondrial DNA had already said which was which. It comes only from the mother, and it was Neanderthal. So the mother was a Neanderthal, and the father was a Denisovan.

The bone could tell a little more. Its thickness showed that the person was at least 13 years old. The DNA showed that she was a girl. She had lived about 90,000 years ago. The team gave her a nickname, Denny.

Her DNA held two more surprises. Her mother was more closely related to Neanderthals who lived far to the west, in what is now Croatia, than to an earlier Neanderthal from her own cave. So Neanderthals had travelled thousands of kilometres across Europe and Asia. And her Denisovan father had a Neanderthal ancestor of his own, hundreds of generations before him. So Denny's parents were not the first such pair.
When Svante Pääbo, the head of the laboratory, first saw the result, he also thought someone had made a mistake. Then he saw the checks. The team published the genome in 2018.

Nobody knows what Denny's real name was, or what words she heard from her mother and her father. Everything known about her came from a splinter that had been put away as unidentifiable. It was found because one student tested every piece.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn in this story is the question 'mistake, or real?' Half Neanderthal and half Denisovan DNA could come from a mix-up, from a long-mixed family, or from a child with one parent of each kind. Viviane Slon separated these by repeating the test six times and then by looking at how the DNA was arranged. In a first-generation child, every pair of chromosomes has one copy from each parent, all the way along. This is the same idea as the Shrinking Pieces Test: unbroken stretches mean the mixing was very recent. The story also shows two habits of good science. Samantha Brown tested all 2,315 pieces when most would have stopped. Viviane Slon doubted her own surprising result first.
ask: A splinter of deer bone and a splinter of human bone look the same. How can collagen tell them apart?
Why did the mitochondrial DNA, taken alone, give only half of the answer?
Viviane Slon's first thought was that she had made a mistake. Why is that a good first thought for a scientist?
How does the pattern 'one copy of each kind, all the way along' show that the parents were of two different kinds?
Denny's father also had a Neanderthal ancestor. What does that tell you about how often these peoples met?

games.title: Who Left This? The six humans game
games.context: This is a card game about six kinds of humans. Each card gives one real clue, such as a bone, a place or a piece of DNA. You work out which kind of human the clue belongs to.

printables.title: 18 clue cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: My jaw has a bony chin that sticks out.
items.b: Homo sapiens. Only our species has a chin like this.

items.f: The oldest known bones on my line are from Morocco. They are about 315,000 years old.
items.b: Homo sapiens. The bones come from Jebel Irhoud.

items.f: My kind is the only kind of human alive today.
items.b: Homo sapiens. The others were gone by about 30,000 to 40,000 years ago.

items.f: My skull is long and low, with a thick ridge over the eyes. My brain is as big as yours.
items.b: Neanderthal. The skull shape is different from ours, but the brain is not smaller.

items.f: My kind's bones were first recognised in a valley in Germany in 1856.
items.b: Neanderthal. The Neander Valley gave them their name.

items.f: People outside Africa carry about 2 percent of my kind's DNA.
items.b: Neanderthal. Our ancestors and Neanderthals had children together about 47,000 years ago.

items.f: Scientists learned that my kind existed from the DNA in one finger bone.
items.b: Denisovan. The finger bone was found in Denisova Cave in Siberia in 2008.

items.f: A gene from my kind helps many Tibetan people cope with thin mountain air.
items.b: Denisovan. The gene is called EPAS1.

items.f: My jaw was found in a cave about 3,300 metres up on the Tibetan Plateau.
items.b: Denisovan. The jaw was matched to Denisovans in 2019, from proteins.

items.f: I am a grown woman, and I am about 1.06 metres tall.
items.b: Homo floresiensis. Her skeleton was found on the island of Flores in 2003.

items.f: I lived on an island in Indonesia, alongside small relatives of elephants.
items.b: Homo floresiensis. The small elephant relatives are called Stegodon.

items.f: My ancestors were probably larger. Over many generations on an island with little food, my kind became small.
items.b: Homo floresiensis. Some scientists think instead that the ancestors were already small.

items.f: My kind's bones lay deep in a cave in South Africa, behind a very narrow passage.
items.b: Homo naledi. Six women scientists who could fit through brought the bones out.

items.f: My brain was less than half the size of yours. Yet I lived only about 300,000 years ago.
items.b: Homo naledi. A small brain and our own species existed at the same time.

items.f: More than 1,550 pieces of bone from at least 15 of my kind came out of one cave chamber.
items.b: Homo naledi. The cave is called Rising Star.

items.f: My kind was named in 2019, from a cave on an island in the Philippines.
items.b: Homo luzonensis. The cave is Callao Cave on the island of Luzon.

items.f: I had small teeth, and curved finger and toe bones.
items.b: Homo luzonensis. Curved bones like these suggest that they climbed.

items.f: Only a few teeth and small bones of my kind have been found, from at least three individuals.
items.b: Homo luzonensis. So little is known that almost everything about them is still open.

If you were wrong, put the card under the right name card. Nobody wins it.

games.title: Only Us? The claim cards
games.context: This is a card game about what makes our kind of human different. Each card names something people have called 'only human'. You decide whether the evidence agrees.

printables.title: 16 claim cards to cut out (the verdict is on the back)

items.f: Making tools
items.b: Not only us. Chimpanzees crack nuts with stones, crows bend twigs into hooks, and other humans made stone tools long before our species existed.

items.f: Using fire
items.b: Not only us. Neanderthals kept fires, and older humans used fire before them.

items.f: Caring for an injured friend for years
items.b: Not only us. A Neanderthal man from Shanidar Cave lived for years with a useless arm and a damaged eye. Others must have helped him.

items.f: Burying the dead
items.b: Not only us, most scientists think. Neanderthals buried at least some of their dead.

items.f: Having a chin
items.b: Only us. No other human and no other ape has a chin that sticks out. Nobody is sure what the chin is for.

items.f: Writing
items.b: Only us, as far as we know. Writing is only about 5,000 years old, so the other humans were gone long before.

items.f: Speaking in sentences
items.b: Nobody knows. Neanderthals had the same version of a speech gene, FOXP2, as we have. But speech leaves no fossil.

items.f: Painting animals on rock
items.b: Only us, as far as we know. The oldest known pictures of animals, in Sulawesi in Indonesia, are more than 45,000 years old and are credited to our species.

items.f: Making marks on cave walls
items.b: Argued about. Red marks in three Spanish caves were dated to before our species arrived. Some scientists doubt the dating.

items.f: Living high in the mountains, where the air is thin
items.b: Not only us. Denisovans lived on the Tibetan Plateau, about 3,300 metres up, at least 160,000 years ago.

items.f: Reaching islands across the sea
items.b: Not only us. The ancestors of Homo floresiensis reached Flores more than 700,000 years ago. Nobody knows how they crossed.

items.f: Having a brain as large as ours
items.b: Not only us. Neanderthal brains were as large as ours, and a little larger on average.

items.f: Spreading to every continent
items.b: Only us. No other kind of human reached Australia or the Americas, as far as anyone has found.

items.f: Teaching the young
items.b: Not only us. Meerkats teach their pups to handle scorpions. Teaching with words is ours alone, as far as we know.

items.f: Making glue
items.b: Not only us. Neanderthals heated birch bark to make a sticky tar and used it to fix stone points to handles.

items.f: Laughing
items.b: Not only us. Young chimpanzees, gorillas, bonobos and orangutans laugh when they are tickled.

If you gave a true example, the other players give you one more tally mark, even if your verdict was different.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The highest total wins.

experiments.title: The Shrinking Pieces Test: what happens to one ancestor's DNA over the generations?
experiments.question: One ancestor gives a child a whole chromosome. After four more generations, how much of that chromosome is left in the family, and is the same piece left in every family line?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After four more generations, how much of the red chromosome will the youngest child have: all of it, half, a small piece or none? Will all six family lines end up the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every family line starts with the same chromosome of 20 red squares. Every line follows the same two rules for the same number of generations. Each chit goes back into the cup after it is pulled, so every cut place has the same chance on every turn. The only thing that differs between the six lines is chance.
results_table: Which squares are red in row 5

materials.item: squared paper from a maths notebook, or plain paper with a grid you rule yourself
a red sketch pen or colour pencil
small paper chits numbered 1 to 19, folded, in a steel tumbler or cup

experiments.record: For each of the six family lines, write the number of red squares at the end of every row. Under the last block, draw one more row called All Together. Colour a square red there if that square is red in row 5 of any line.
experiments.context: In this experiment a row of 20 squares stands for one chromosome, and red stands for DNA from one ancestor. You pass the chromosome down five generations in six family lines, using a coin and number chits. It shows what happened to Neanderthal DNA inside our ancestors' families.
