flow.do: 1. Explain the model. A row of 20 squares is one chromosome. Red is DNA from one ancestor, and white is DNA from everyone else. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: A red ancestor has a child. That child has children, and so on for four more generations. How much red will the youngest child have? Will every family line end the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A red ancestor passes on a red chromosome. Guess how much red is left after four more generations. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the red will, or will not, stay the same?
good: It will halve each time, because each parent gives half.
It will stay, because DNA is copied exactly.
It will get mixed up with the white.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect the red to spread out as a pale pink, or to stay whole. Both guesses are worth testing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shrinking Pieces Test. Here you guess what happens to one ancestor's DNA.

flow.do: 1. On squared paper, mark out a block 20 squares wide and 5 rows deep. 2. Number the columns 1 to 20. 3. Draw five more blocks the same, with a gap between blocks. 4. Label the blocks A to F. 5. Write the numbers 1 to 19 on chits, fold them and put them in a cup.
flow.say: Each block is one family line. Row 1 is the child of the red ancestor. Row 5 is that child's great-great-grandchild.
flow.kid: Draw six blocks. Each block is 20 squares wide and 5 rows deep. Number the columns. Make chits numbered 1 to 19.
flow.parent: If your notebook has small squares, use two squares for each one so the rows are easy to colour. Share the drawing: three blocks each is quicker.
flow.context: In this step of the Shrinking Pieces Test you draw six family lines and make the number chits.

flow.do: 1. In block A, colour all 20 squares of row 1 red. 2. Pull a chit, say 8. Draw a small line after square 8 in row 2. 3. Toss the coin. 4. Heads: copy the left side of the row above, squares 1 to 8. Leave the right side white. 5. Tails: leave the left side white. Copy the right side of the row above, squares 9 to 20. 6. Put the chit back.
flow.say: The chit is where the chromosome crosses over. The coin decides which side comes from the red family. The other side comes from the white partner, so it is white.
flow.kid: Colour row 1 red. Pull a chit and mark the cut. Heads, copy the left side. Tails, copy the right side. Leave the other side white.
flow.parent: 'Copy' means the same colours as the row directly above, square for square. From row 3 on, the row above is part white, so the copied side may be part white or all white.
flow.context: In this step of the Shrinking Pieces Test you make the first new generation together, to learn the two rules.

flow.do: 1. Finish block A: do rows 3, 4 and 5 the same way, each copied from the row just above. 2. Write the number of red squares at the end of every row. 3. Do blocks B to F the same way.
flow.say: Each new row is the next generation. Pull a chit, toss the coin, copy one side from the row above. Count the red squares each time.
flow.kid: Do rows 3, 4 and 5. Each row copies from the row above. Count the red squares. Then do blocks B to F.

ask.q: What do you notice about the red as you go down a block?
good: It gets shorter, or stays the same, but never longer.
Sometimes it all goes at once.
It stays in one piece.

flow.parent: If a line loses all its red, the rows below stay white. Fill them in quickly and move on. That line is a result too, so do not start it again.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Shrinking Pieces Test. Here you pass the chromosome down four more generations in six family lines.

flow.do: 1. Count how many of the six lines still have red in row 5. 2. Compare the red pieces that are left. Are they the same squares? 3. Draw the All Together row. Colour a square red if any line has it red in row 5.
flow.say: How many lines kept some red? Did they keep the same squares? Now colour the All Together row and count the red there.
flow.kid: Count the lines that still have red. Are the red squares the same ones? Colour the All Together row.
flow.parent: Usually one, two or three lines of six keep a little red in row 5, and the pieces sit in different places. If all six lines are white in row 5, use row 4 for the All Together row. That happens about one time in eight.
flow.context: In this step of the Shrinking Pieces Test you compare the six family lines and add their pieces together.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Have them write the claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 3. Only then read the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Tell me your claim about what happens to one ancestor's DNA. What did you see that supports it? Why do you think the lines ended differently?
flow.kid: Write your claim. Write what you saw in the six blocks. Write why you think it happened.

ask.q: No single line kept much red. Why does the All Together row have more?
good: Different lines kept different pieces.
Adding many people's pieces gives back more of the ancestor.

ask.q: A scientist finds a person with one very long red piece. What does that say about when the red ancestor lived?
good: Not long ago, because the piece has not been cut much.
Only a few generations back.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. When a body makes an egg or sperm cell, each pair of chromosomes crosses over and swaps parts. So an ancestor's piece is cut shorter in each generation, and chance decides whether any is passed on. This happened to Neanderthal DNA. Each person outside Africa has only short pieces, about 2 percent in all, and different people have different pieces. Joined together, the pieces of many people give back about half of a Neanderthal genome. The model is simplified in two ways. Real chromosomes may cross over in two or three places. And in the model every partner was all white, so the red share kept halving. In real life, after the mixing, most partners carried some pieces too, so the share stayed near 2 percent.

check.q: Why does a piece of an ancestor's DNA get shorter over the generations?
options: Crossing over swaps part of it away
The child's body uses it up
check.why: In each generation the chromosome crosses over with a partner chromosome, so part of the ancestor's piece is replaced. Choosing 'wears thin' or 'uses it up' treats DNA like a pencil that gets shorter with use. The DNA is copied whole each time, and only the swapping cuts the piece.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Shrinking Pieces Test. Here you say what you found and what it means for Neanderthal DNA in people today.

experiments.title: The Teaching Test: is a skill learned better by watching, or by watching with words?
experiments.question: A new learner has to fold a paper cup that holds 15 channa. Does the learner do better after only looking at a finished cup, after watching it being folded in silence, or after watching with spoken teaching?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which learner will make the best cup: the one who only looks, the one who watches, or the one who is taught with words? Or will all do the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every learner gets the same size of paper, sees the fold only once and has the same four minutes. No learner has made this cup before, and no learner watches another learner. Only one thing changes: how the skill is passed on. People differ in how easily they fold paper, so one person for each way is a small test. Two people for each way is better.
results_table: How the skill was passed on

materials.item: square sheets of paper about 15 centimetres wide, cut from old newspaper or notebook pages
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
learners who have never folded this cup: family, friends or neighbours. Two are enough, and three are better. A video call also works

experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each learner. Write how the skill was passed on, whether the cup was finished in four minutes, the time, whether it held 15 channa, and which fold went wrong.
experiments.context: In this experiment you teach the same paper fold to different people in different ways, and compare how well the skill is passed on. It tests one idea about what helped our kind of human: teaching with words. Scientists ran a larger test like this in 2015, with stone tools.

setup.art: A square of paper folded corner to corner into a triangle, lying with the long folded edge at the bottom and the point at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the square into a triangle. Put the long edge at the bottom.

setup.art: The triangle with the bottom left corner folded across so the corner's tip touches the right sloping edge, and the top edge of the flap lying level.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the left corner across to the right edge. Keep the flap's top edge level.

setup.art: The same shape with the bottom right corner folded across over the first flap to touch the left edge, leaving two loose triangle flaps at the top.
setup.caption: 3. Fold the right corner across in the same way.

setup.art: The front top flap folded down over the front, the back top flap folded down behind, and the pocket opened into a cup holding channa.
setup.caption: 4. Fold one top flap down in front and one behind. Open the cup.

setup.art: A girl folding paper slowly at a table while an older man watches from across the table with his own blank square ready.
setup.caption: 5. Teach each learner in a different way. Time each one.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from three learners

flow.do: 1. Your child learns the cup from the four step pictures. 2. They fold it three times, until it holds 15 channa every time. 3. Keep the best cup as the model.
flow.say: First you must become the expert. Fold the cup three times. Which fold is the hardest to get right?
flow.kid: Learn the paper cup from the pictures. Fold it three times. Keep your best cup.
flow.parent: The hard fold is the second one. The corner's tip must touch the opposite sloping edge, and the top of the flap must lie level. If it slopes, the cup will not lock.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Teaching Test. Here you learn the paper cup well enough to teach it.

flow.do: 1. Explain the three ways of passing on the skill: looking only, watching, and watching with words. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write both down.
flow.say: One learner only looks at your finished cup. One watches you fold in silence. One watches while you explain. Who will do best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three learners, three ways. Guess who will make the best cup. Say why.

ask.q: What might a learner miss if nobody says anything?
good: That the flap's top edge must be level.
Where exactly the corner should touch.
Which way to fold the last flaps.

flow.parent: With only two learners, leave out 'looking only'. Compare watching in silence with watching with words.
flow.context: In this step of the Teaching Test you guess which way of passing on a skill works best.

flow.do: 1. Learner 1 looks at the finished cup for one minute. They may turn it over but not unfold it. 2. Learner 2 watches your child fold one cup slowly, in silence, with no pointing or nodding. 3. Learner 3 watches one fold while your child explains, and may ask questions. 4. After each showing, the learner gets one square and four minutes. Time them. 5. Test each cup with 15 channa. Lift it and shake it gently three times.
flow.say: Each learner comes in alone, so nobody learns from watching the others. You show the fold only once. Then start the timer.
flow.kid: Bring in one learner at a time. Show the fold once, in that learner's way. Time them. Test the cup with 15 channa.
flow.parent: Keep the other learners in another room. Staying silent is hard, so remind your child before learner 2 comes in. Write down which fold went wrong, because that is the most useful result.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Teaching Test. Here each learner is shown the fold in a different way and then tries it.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Have them write the claim, the evidence and the reasoning. 3. Only then read the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Tell me your claim. Which results support it? Why do you think that way of passing on the skill worked best?
flow.kid: Write your claim. Write what each learner managed. Write why you think it happened.

ask.q: Which fold went wrong most often? Could it be learned by watching alone?
good: The second fold. You can see it, but not what matters about it.
Words can say 'keep this edge level', and watching cannot.

ask.q: Is one learner for each way enough to be sure?
good: No. One person may just be good at folding.
We should test more people, or swap the learners with a new fold.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. In 2015, Thomas Morgan and his team taught 184 people to chip simple stone tools. The skill was passed down chains of learners. It survived well only when learners were taught, and best when they were taught with words. Words can point out what matters and what to avoid. The team suggests that as tools became harder to make, teaching and language became more useful. Your result may differ. With an easy fold, a careful watcher often succeeds without words. Report what you found.

check.q: What can spoken teaching pass on that silent watching cannot?
options: The shape of the finished thing
How fast the teacher's hands move
check.why: A watcher can see the shape, the order and the speed. Words add what cannot be seen: which part must be exact, and what goes wrong if it is not. Choosing 'the order of the steps' misses that a watcher sees the order too.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Teaching Test. Here you say what you found and what it suggests about teaching and language.

activities.title: Four Clues on Your Own Skull
activities.context: In this activity you feel four parts of your own skull and compare them with a Neanderthal skull. Scientists use the same four clues to tell which kind of human a fossil skull belonged to.
activities.record: Draw two heads from the side: your own and a Neanderthal's. Label the chin, the brow, the forehead and the back of the head on both.

setup.art: A girl pressing two fingers on the bony bump of her chin while looking in a mirror.
setup.caption: 1. Feel your chin, your brow, your forehead and the back of your head.

setup.art: Two skulls seen from the side: one tall and round with a chin and a smooth brow, one long and low with no chin, a thick brow ridge and a bulge at the back.
setup.caption: 2. Compare with a Neanderthal skull.

setup.art: A child's drawing of two side-view heads with four labels on each.
setup.caption: 3. Draw both heads from the side and label the four clues.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses a finger under the lower lip and slides it down. They feel for a bony bump at the front of the jaw. 2. They run a finger across the bone above the eyes. 3. They put a flat hand on the forehead. 4. They cup a hand round the back of the head.
flow.say: What do you notice at the front of your jaw? Is the bone above your eyes thick or thin? Does your forehead slope back or go straight up?
flow.kid: Feel the bump on your chin. Feel the bone over your eyes. Feel your forehead. Feel the back of your head.

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: My chin sticks out in a bump.
My forehead goes straight up.
The back of my head is round.
Why do we have a chin at all?

flow.context: This is the first step of Four Clues on Your Own Skull. Here you feel four parts of your own head.

flow.do: 1. Read the four Neanderthal clues aloud from the note. 2. Your child compares each with their own head, using the picture. 3. They draw both heads from the side and label the four clues.
flow.say: A Neanderthal jaw sloped back with no chin. A thick ridge of bone ran over the eyes. The forehead was low and sloping. The skull was long, with a bulge at the back.
flow.kid: A Neanderthal had no chin and a thick brow ridge. The forehead sloped. The skull was long. Draw both heads.
flow.parent: The four clues: chin or no chin, thin brow or thick brow ridge, upright or sloping forehead, round or long skull. A Neanderthal skull was not smaller. It held a brain as big as ours, in a different shape.
flow.context: In this step of Four Clues on Your Own Skull you compare your head with a Neanderthal skull and draw both.

flow.do: 1. Ask what a skull can tell, and what it cannot. 2. Make two short lists together.
flow.say: A scientist finds a jaw with a clear chin. Which kind of human is it? Now tell me three things about that person that the jaw cannot tell us.
flow.kid: A jaw has a chin. Whose jaw is it? Name three things the jaw cannot tell you.

ask.q: What can a skull not tell us?
good: Skin and hair colour.
What language the person spoke.
What they thought or felt.
Who their parents were.

check.q: A fossil jaw has a bony chin that sticks out. Which kind of human is it most likely from?
check.why: A chin that sticks out is found only in our species. Neanderthal jaws slope back. Choosing 'any kind' misses that some features belong to one kind only, which is why scientists look for them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Four Clues on Your Own Skull. Here you decide what a skull can and cannot tell.

activities.title: Whose Child? Read the DNA pairs
activities.context: In this activity you work out who the parents of three mystery children were, from pairs of DNA markers. It is a simple version of how scientists found out that a girl called Denny had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
activities.record: For each bone, write who you think the two parents were, and the pattern that told you.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three rows of twelve boxes, each box holding two letters such as NN or ND, and the rows labelled Bone 1, Bone 2 and Bone 3.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the three rows of marker pairs.

setup.art: The same rows with every N coloured blue and every D coloured orange, so that one row is all blue, one is half and half in every box, and one is blue with a short orange patch.
setup.caption: 2. Colour N in one colour and D in another. Look at the pattern.

setup.art: A child writing 'mother' and 'father' under one of the rows, with a small loop labelled 'from mother only' drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Decide who the parents were. Use the mother-only DNA to say which was which.

example_chart.title: The marker pairs of three mystery bones (N is the Neanderthal kind, D is the Denisovan kind)
cols: The 12 marker places, in order along one chromosome
rows: NN NN NN NN NN NN NN NN NN NN NN NN
ND ND ND ND ND ND ND ND ND ND ND ND
NN NN ND ND ND NN NN NN NN NN NN NN

flow.do: 1. Explain the markers. At some places in the DNA, Neanderthals always had one letter and Denisovans always had another. Call them N and D. 2. A child has two copies of each place, one from each parent. 3. Your child copies the three rows from the table and colours N and D differently.
flow.say: Every box is one place in the DNA. The two letters are the two copies, one from the mother and one from the father. What patterns do you notice?
flow.kid: Each box has two letters, one from each parent. Copy the three rows. Colour N and D differently.
flow.parent: Bone 1 is NN at all 12 places. Bone 2 is ND at all 12 places. Bone 3 is NN at places 1 and 2, ND at places 3, 4 and 5, and NN at places 6 to 12.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose Child. Here you copy the marker pairs of three mystery bones.

flow.do: 1. Ask who the parents of each child were. 2. Let your child reason aloud before you help. 3. Write the answers.
flow.say: A Neanderthal parent can give only N. A Denisovan parent can give only D. So who were the parents of Bone 1? Of Bone 2? What is odd about Bone 3?
flow.kid: A Neanderthal parent gives N. A Denisovan parent gives D. Work out the parents of each bone.

ask.q: Bone 3 is mostly NN, with one short patch of ND. How could that happen?
good: One parent was a Neanderthal with a Denisovan ancestor long before.
The D piece is what is left after crossing over cut it short.

flow.parent: Bone 1: two Neanderthal parents. Bone 2: one Neanderthal parent and one Denisovan parent, because every place has one of each. Bone 3: two mostly Neanderthal parents, one of whom carried a short Denisovan piece from an ancestor several generations back.
flow.context: In this step of Whose Child you work out the parents from the pattern of pairs.

flow.do: 1. Point to the last column. Mother-only DNA is mitochondrial DNA, which comes from the mother alone. 2. Ask which parent of Bone 2 was the Neanderthal.
flow.say: Bone 2 had one Neanderthal parent and one Denisovan parent. The mother-only DNA is N. So which parent was which?
flow.kid: The mother-only DNA of Bone 2 is N. Which parent was the Neanderthal?
flow.parent: The mother was the Neanderthal and the father the Denisovan. Bone 2 is Denny's real pattern, made simple. Scientists used many thousands of marker places, not 12.

check.q: A child has one N and one D at every marker place. Who were the parents?
check.why: One copy of each kind at every place means each parent could give only one kind. Two parents from long-mixed families would give patches of NN and DD as well, because crossing over mixes the pieces.

flow.context: This is the last step of Whose Child. Here you use the mother-only DNA to say which parent was which.

activities.title: The Shredded Message: read a sentence from short pieces
activities.context: In this activity a sentence is cut into short pieces and mixed with pieces of a different sentence. You rebuild it from the overlaps. Scientists read ancient DNA in the same way, because old DNA is in short pieces and mixed with the DNA of microbes.

materials.item: strips of paper about 30 centimetres long and 2 centimetres wide

activities.safety: Use child-safe scissors, or let a grown-up cut.
activities.record: Write the sentence you rebuilt, how long it took, and how many pieces did not belong.

setup.art: Three paper strips with the same sentence in capital letters, each strip cut at different places into short pieces, and a fourth strip with a different sentence also cut up.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up writes the sentence on three strips and cuts each at different places.

setup.art: A bowl full of mixed short paper pieces with letters on them.
setup.caption: 2. Mix all the pieces in a bowl, with the pieces of the second sentence.

setup.art: A girl laying paper pieces in rows on the floor so that the letters of one piece line up under the same letters of another.
setup.caption: 3. Rebuild the sentence by finding pieces that overlap.

flow.do: 1. Out of your child's sight, write ONE YOUNG FAMILY FROM AFRICA in capitals on three strips. 2. Cut each strip into pieces of 4 to 6 letters, at different places on each strip. Cut through the middle of words. 3. Write MICROBES LIVE IN OLD BONES on the fourth strip and cut it up too. 4. Mix all the pieces in the bowl.
flow.say: These pieces are like the DNA in an old bone. The message is there, but it is in short pieces. Some pieces come from something else.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts up a secret sentence. Some pieces are from another sentence. All go in the bowl.
flow.parent: Cutting each copy at different places is what makes overlaps. Without overlaps the pieces cannot be put in order. If your child is alone, they can prepare the puzzle for you and time you.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Shredded Message. Here a grown-up makes the puzzle.

flow.do: 1. Your child tips out the pieces and rebuilds the sentence. 2. They lay overlapping pieces one under another, with the same letters lined up. 3. They put pieces that fit nowhere in a separate pile. 4. Time it.
flow.say: Find two pieces that share some letters. Line the shared letters up. Keep going until one sentence runs from start to end.
flow.kid: Find pieces that share letters. Line them up. Build the whole sentence. Put odd pieces aside.

ask.q: How did you know a piece did not belong?
good: It did not overlap with anything.
It made a different word.

flow.parent: Expect about 15 to 18 true pieces and 5 or 6 that do not belong. Three copies mean most letters are covered three times, so one torn or smudged piece does no harm.
flow.context: In this step of The Shredded Message you rebuild the sentence from overlapping pieces.

flow.do: 1. Mix the true pieces again. 2. Write the whole sentence on a fresh strip and lay it on the floor as a guide. 3. Your child places the pieces under the guide. Time it again.
flow.say: Now you have a guide to lay the pieces against. Is it faster? Scientists use a genome from a person of today as their guide.
flow.kid: Now use the full sentence as a guide. Place the pieces under it. Is it faster?
flow.parent: It is much faster with a guide. Explain the catch: a guide from a living person can hide the places where the ancient person truly differed. So every difference is checked against many pieces.

check.q: Why do scientists read each place in ancient DNA many times, from many pieces?
options: One piece may be damaged or foreign
To make the bone last longer
check.why: Old DNA is damaged, and some pieces come from microbes or from people who touched the bone. If many separate pieces agree, the letter can be trusted. Choosing 'adds new DNA' mixes up reading with making.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Shredded Message. Here you rebuild the sentence again with a guide, as scientists do.

activities.title: Warm or Cold: why does old DNA last in cold caves?
activities.context: In this activity you time the same fizzing reaction in cold, room and warm water. It shows a rule of chemistry that explains why ancient DNA is found in cold caves and almost never in hot places.

materials.item: steel tumblers or glasses of the same size
fruit salt, such as ENO. Or mix half a teaspoon of baking soda with half a teaspoon of citric acid crystals for each tumbler
water from the fridge, water at room temperature, and warm water

activities.safety: A grown-up prepares the warm water. It should be as warm as bath water, never hot enough to hurt a finger.
activities.record: Write the time in seconds for the fizzing to stop in cold, room and warm water.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers in a row, each half full of water, labelled 'cold', 'room' and 'warm', with a faint mist on the cold one.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three tumblers: fridge water, room water and warm water.

setup.art: A hand tipping half a teaspoon of white powder into the first tumbler while another hand starts a phone timer.
setup.caption: 2. Add half a teaspoon of fruit salt. Start the timer.

setup.art: The three tumblers side by side, the warm one fizzing hard and the cold one fizzing gently.
setup.caption: 3. Stop the timer when no more bubbles rise. Do each tumbler in turn.

flow.do: 1. Fill the three tumblers half full: fridge water, room water and warm water. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The powder fizzes when it meets water. That fizz is a chemical reaction. In which water will the fizzing finish first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three tumblers: cold, room and warm. Guess where the fizz will finish first. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Warm or Cold. Here you set up three tumblers and guess.

flow.do: 1. Add half a level teaspoon of fruit salt to the cold tumbler. Start the timer at once. 2. Stop it when no more bubbles rise from the bottom. 3. Write the time. 4. Do the same for the room tumbler and the warm tumbler.
flow.say: Do one tumbler at a time, so you can watch closely. Do not stir, because stirring would change the test.
flow.kid: Add the powder to one tumbler. Time the fizz until the bubbles stop. Write the time. Do all three.
flow.parent: The warm tumbler usually finishes in well under half the time of the cold one. If all three finish too fast to time, use a whole teaspoon and add ice to the cold water.
flow.context: In this step of Warm or Cold you time the fizzing in each tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child saw and why they think it happened. 2. Then explain the link to old DNA.
flow.say: What did you find? Now think of a bone lying in a cave for 50,000 years. Water slowly reacts with the DNA and cuts it. Where would the DNA last longer, in Siberia or in Tamil Nadu?
flow.kid: Which was fastest? Water slowly cuts DNA in old bones. Where would DNA last longer, a cold cave or a hot one?
flow.parent: After your child has answered, explain. Particles move faster when they are warm. They meet more often and hit harder, so they react more often. This is true of nearly every chemical reaction. The reaction that cuts DNA is a different reaction from the fizz, but it follows the same rule. This is one reason why India, with very old stone tools, has given no DNA from ancient humans so far.

check.q: Why has more ancient human DNA been found in Siberia than in South India?
options: More ancient humans lived in Siberia
DNA breaks down more slowly in the cold
check.why: The reactions that cut DNA go more slowly in the cold, so more survives. Choosing 'more humans lived in Siberia' mixes up where people lived with where their DNA lasted. India's stone tools show that ancient humans lived here for more than a million years.

flow.context: This is the last step of Warm or Cold. Here you link the fizz test to DNA in old bones.

activities.title: Who Lived When? Seven kinds of humans on one time line
activities.context: In this activity you draw seven kinds of humans as bars on one time line of the last 350,000 years. Then you count how many kinds were alive at the same moment.

materials.item: a strip of paper 35 centimetres long and about 10 centimetres wide. Tape two notebook pages together if needed

activities.record: Write how many bars your ruler crosses at 300,000, at 100,000 and at 20,000 years ago.

setup.art: A long paper strip with a ruled line along the bottom marked every 5 centimetres, the right end labelled 'today' and the left end labelled '350,000 years ago'.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line 35 centimetres long. One centimetre is 10,000 years.

setup.art: The strip with seven coloured bars of different lengths stacked above the line, some running off the left edge and only one reaching the right end.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one bar for each kind of human.

setup.art: A ruler held upright across the strip at the 10 centimetre mark, crossing five bars.
setup.caption: 3. Stand a ruler across the strip. Count the bars it crosses.

example_chart.title: Where each bar starts and ends, measured from the Today end (1 centimetre is 10,000 years)
rows: Oldest fossils on our line, about 315,000 years
Fossils from about 200,000 to about 32,000 years ago
Last known in Java about 110,000 years ago
The Rising Star bones, 335,000 to 236,000 years
Bones from 100,000 years, tools until about 50,000 years
Bones at least 50,000 years old, perhaps 134,000

flow.do: 1. Draw a straight line 35 centimetres long near the bottom of the strip. 2. Label the right end 'today'. 3. Mark every 5 centimetres. Label the marks 50,000, 100,000 and so on. The left end is 350,000. 4. Ask how many kinds of humans your child thinks lived 100,000 years ago.
flow.say: One centimetre on this line is 10,000 years. Before we draw, guess. How many kinds of humans were alive 100,000 years ago? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a line 35 centimetres long. One centimetre is 10,000 years. Guess how many kinds lived 100,000 years ago.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Lived When. Here you draw the time line and guess.

flow.do: 1. Read each row of the table aloud. 2. Your child measures from the Today end and draws each bar in a different colour, one above another. 3. Use a dotted bar where the table says dotted. 4. Label each bar.
flow.say: Measure from the Today end each time. A dotted bar means scientists are not sure of those dates.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each kind of human. Measure from the Today end. Use dots where the dates are unsure.
flow.parent: A bar shows only the fossils found so far. Each kind surely lived for longer than the bones we happen to have. Say this as you draw.
flow.context: In this step of Who Lived When you draw seven kinds of humans as bars on the time line.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler upright across the strip at 30 centimetres. Count the bars it crosses. 2. Do the same at 10 centimetres and at 2 centimetres. 3. Ask what your child notices.
flow.say: How many kinds were alive 300,000 years ago? 100,000 years ago? 20,000 years ago? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Put the ruler across at 30, at 10 and at 2 centimetres. Count the bars each time.

ask.q: For how much of the line has our kind been the only one?
good: Only the last 3 or 4 centimetres.
About 30,000 to 40,000 years out of 315,000.

flow.parent: At 30 centimetres the ruler crosses four bars: our species, Neanderthals, Homo erectus and Homo naledi. Denisovans were probably alive too, but their bar is dotted there. At 10 centimetres it crosses five, counting the Homo floresiensis bar that starts there: our species, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis. At 2 centimetres it crosses one.

check.q: For how much of our species' time have we been the only kind of human?
check.why: Our species is about 315,000 years old, and the others were gone by about 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. That is roughly one tenth. Choosing 'all of it' follows the old picture of one kind turning into the next, with no overlap.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Lived When. Here you count how many kinds of humans were alive at the same time.

projects.title: The Human Bush: a poster of our family, with the mixing shown
projects.context: In this three-day project you draw the human family of the last 350,000 years as a bush, not a line. You show which kinds lived at the same time, where they had children together, and where the evidence is missing.

materials.item: a large sheet of chart paper
your time line from Who Lived When, if you made it
small paper slips and glue or tape, for labels

schedule.what: Draw the bush. Time runs up the page, from 350,000 years ago at the bottom to today at the top. Draw one branch for each of seven kinds of humans, side by side, and end each branch at the right height.
Add the mixing. Draw an arrow from the Neanderthal branch to ours, one from the Denisovan branch to ours, and one between Neanderthals and Denisovans. Label each arrow with its evidence.
Add an India box with the Narmada skull and the Attirampakkam tools. Put a question mark wherever scientists argue or do not know. Present the poster in three minutes.

projects.record: One poster showing seven branches, three mixing arrows with their evidence, an India box, and at least four question marks with a line on what is unknown at each.

setup.art: A chart paper with a time scale up the left side and seven coloured branches rising side by side, most ending below the top.
setup.caption: 1. Draw seven branches. End each one at the right time.

setup.art: The same poster with three thin arrows crossing between branches, each with a small label such as '2 percent' or 'Denny'.
setup.caption: 2. Add arrows where two kinds had children together.

setup.art: A girl sticking a question mark slip beside a box labelled 'India', which holds a small drawing of a skull top and a hand axe.
setup.caption: 3. Add the India box and the question marks.

flow.do: 1. Draw a time scale up the left edge, from 350,000 years ago to today. 2. check.q: Why is a bush with arrows a better picture of human history than a single line?
options: Several kinds lived together and mixed
A line shows too many kinds
check.why: A line shows one kind turning into the next. The evidence shows several kinds alive at once, with children born between some of them. Choosing 'a line shows too many kinds' has it backwards, because a line hides most of them.

challenges.title: The Clean Sample: take 'bone powder' without leaving a trace of yourself
challenges.context: In this challenge turmeric on your fingers stands for your own DNA, and a biscuit stands for an old bone. You design a way to collect crumbs from inside the biscuit without any yellow reaching the sample. Scientists who read ancient DNA face the same problem.
challenges.problem: Your fingertips are covered in turmeric. Collect half a teaspoon of crumbs from the inside of a biscuit into a clean bowl, with no yellow on the crumbs, the bowl or the white paper under it.
constraints: You may not wash or wipe your hands once the turmeric is on.
The crumbs must come from the inside of the biscuit, not from its surface.
You may use only the materials listed.
You have 15 minutes for planning and two tries.
materials: half a teaspoon of turmeric powder on a saucer
3 plain biscuits, such as Marie biscuits
a small steel bowl standing on a sheet of white paper
2 small clean plastic bags or a piece of cling film
old newspaper to cover the table
general: Cover your hands. Put a clean plastic bag over each hand, as scientists wear gloves.
Touch the biscuit only with tools. Hold it with one spoon and scrape with the other.
Throw away the surface. Break the biscuit and take crumbs only from the fresh inside, as scientists drill past the surface of a bone.
creative: Run a blank. Handle a second, empty bowl in exactly the same way, and check it for yellow. Laboratories do this to catch contamination they cannot see.
Change gloves between steps, so that yellow picked up from the outside of the biscuit does not reach the bowl.
Work in one direction: dirty things on the left, clean things on the right, and never move anything back.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own clean method and write it as numbered steps that someone else could follow. Then say where a trace of yellow could still get in, and how you would check.
challenges.safety: Turmeric stains cloth and some tabletops. Cover the table with newspaper and wear old clothes.

flow.parent: Let the first plan be your child's own, even if you can see where it will fail. The failure shows where contamination gets in.

flow.do: 1. Your child carries out the plan with the first biscuit. 2. Lift the bowl and look at the white paper. 3. Look at the crumbs, the bowl's rim and the tools for yellow.

flow.context: In this step of The Clean Sample you make your first try and trace where the yellow went.

flow.do: 1. Your child changes the plan to block each path the yellow took. 2. They try again with a new biscuit and fresh white paper. 3. They also handle an empty second bowl the same way, as a blank.
flow.say: Change one thing for each place the yellow reached. This time, treat an empty bowl the same way too. What will the empty bowl tell us?
flow.kid: Fix your plan. Try again with a new biscuit. Treat an empty bowl the same way.
flow.parent: The empty bowl is a blank. If yellow turns up in the blank, the method itself is carrying contamination, whatever the sample looks like.
flow.context: In this step of The Clean Sample you improve the method and add a blank.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two tries. 2. Read how real laboratories work, from the note. 3. Your child writes their final method as numbered steps.
flow.say: Which change helped most? Now write your method so that someone else could follow it exactly.
flow.kid: Which change helped most? Write your clean method as numbered steps.
flow.parent: Real ancient DNA laboratories use sealed rooms with filtered air. Workers wear full suits, masks and two pairs of gloves. They clean or remove the bone's surface, drill from the inside, and run blanks beside every sample. Even so, early studies were often fooled by modern DNA.

check.q: Why do scientists take bone powder from inside a bone, not from its surface?
options: The inside is softer to drill
The surface has no bone in it
Inside powder is a nicer colour
The surface carries DNA from people and microbes
check.why: Everyone who has handled the bone has left skin cells on the surface, and microbes live there too. The inside is better protected. Choosing 'softer to drill' picks a reason of comfort, when the real reason is contamination.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Clean Sample. Here you compare your method with a real laboratory's.

items.p: About how many kinds of humans were alive 100,000 years ago?
items.why: Our species, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis were all alive then. Choosing 'only one' follows the old picture of a single line.

items.p: The kind of human who lived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago is called the ____.
a: Neanderthal
Neanderthals
items.why: Neanderthals lived across Europe and western and central Asia. They are named after the Neander Valley in Germany.

items.p: True or false: the kinds of humans came one after another in a single line, never two at once.
items.why: False. Dated fossils show several kinds alive at the same time. The family is a branching bush.

items.p: Match each kind of human to where their fossils were found.
items.why: Each kind is known from a different part of the world. Only our species spread to every continent.

items.p: Which feature of the skeleton is found only in our species?
items.why: Only Homo sapiens has a chin that sticks out. Neanderthals had brains as large as ours, and all these humans walked upright and had thumbs.

items.p: Sort each one: can a fossil bone or tooth show it?
items.why: Bones and teeth record size, age and injuries. Soft parts, words and thoughts leave nothing in bone.
cats: A bone or tooth can show it
A bone or tooth cannot show it
items: A bone or tooth can show it
A bone or tooth can show it
A bone or tooth can show it
A bone or tooth cannot show it
A bone or tooth cannot show it
A bone or tooth cannot show it

items.p: True or false: Neanderthals had smaller brains than people today.
items.why: False. Neanderthal brains were as large as ours, and a little larger on average.

items.p: The complete set of DNA instructions of one living being is called a ____.
a: genome
items.why: A human genome has about 3 billion DNA letters. The first rough Neanderthal genome was read in 2010.

items.p: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, the red piece got shorter down each block. Explain why.
items.a: Each new row was made by crossing over. One side was copied from the row above, and the other side came from a white partner. So part of the red was swapped for white in each generation, and it could never grow back.
items.why: A strong answer names crossing over, and says that only one side is copied from the family's chromosome.

items.p: Why is ancient DNA found mostly in cold places?
opts: DNA breaks down more slowly in the cold
Ancient humans lived only in cold places
items.why: The reactions that cut DNA go more slowly in the cold. Ancient humans lived in hot places too, as India's stone tools show, but their DNA has not lasted.

items.p: Put these in order, from longest ago to most recent.
a: The oldest known fossils on our line
Denny, the girl with parents of two kinds, lives
Most of the mixing between our ancestors and Neanderthals
Neanderthals are gone as a separate people
The first Neanderthal genome is read
items.why: The fossils are about 315,000 years old. Denny lived about 90,000 years ago, the mixing was about 47,000 years ago, Neanderthals were gone by about 40,000, and the genome was read in 2010.
items: Neanderthals are gone as a separate people
The first Neanderthal genome is read
The oldest known fossils on our line
Most of the mixing between our ancestors and Neanderthals
Denny, the girl with parents of two kinds, lives

items.p: Draw a Neanderthal skull and a skull of our species from the side. Label two differences.
items.a: The Neanderthal skull is long and low, with a thick brow ridge, a sloping forehead and no chin. Ours is tall and round, with a smooth brow, an upright forehead and a chin.
items.why: A strong drawing shows at least two of the four clues: chin, brow, forehead and the shape of the skull.
items.art: Two blank side-view head outlines with label lines.

items.p: About how much of the DNA of people outside Africa came from Neanderthals?
items.why: It is about 2 percent, in thousands of short pieces. Choosing 50 percent mixes up people today with a child of the first generation.

items.p: True or false: a child gets mitochondrial DNA only from the mother.
items.why: True. Mitochondria are passed on in the egg cell. That is why this DNA can show who the mother's family was.

items.p: India has stone tools more than a million years old. Why do we not know who made them?
items.a: Stone lasts, but bones rarely become fossils, and almost no bones have been found with the tools. India is also warm, so no ancient DNA has been recovered. Without bones or DNA, the tools cannot be matched to a kind of human.
items.why: A strong answer says that tools show someone was there, and that only bones or DNA can say who.

items.p: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, all six lines followed the same rules. Why did they end differently?
opts: Some lines started with less red
Red squares are weaker than white
Chance chose each cut place and side
items.why: The chit and the coin were different each time, so each line lost different parts. Every line began with the same 20 red squares.

items.p: Each person has about 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. How can living people together hold about half a Neanderthal genome?
items.a: Different people carry different pieces, because chance decided which pieces each family line kept. When the pieces from thousands of people are laid side by side, they cover much more of the genome than any one person's pieces do.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pieces differ from person to person, as the All Together row showed.

items.p: When a pair of chromosomes swaps parts while an egg or sperm cell is made, it is called crossing ____.
a: over
items.why: Crossing over gives each child a new mix of the grandparents' DNA, and cuts old pieces shorter.

items.p: True or false: one very long piece of Neanderthal DNA means a Neanderthal ancestor only a few generations back.
items.why: True. Crossing over cuts pieces shorter in every generation, so a long unbroken piece has not been through many generations.

items.p: A child has one Neanderthal copy and one Denisovan copy at every marker place. Who were the parents?
items.why: Each parent gave one copy at every place. One could give only the Neanderthal kind and the other only the Denisovan kind.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.why: These are the main words for reading old DNA. A strong answer can also give an example of each.
pairs: DNA from outside mixed into a sample
a child of parents from two kinds

items.p: Sort each finding: was it learned from the shape of bones, or from DNA?
items.why: Bones show bodies and injuries. DNA shows who was related to whom. The full story needs both.
items: Homo floresiensis was about a metre tall
People outside Africa carry Neanderthal pieces
A Neanderthal man lived on after bad injuries
Denisovans were a group of their own

items.p: Three of these make ancient DNA hard to read. Which is the odd one out?
opts: It is in very short pieces
People who touched the bone left DNA
It has more than four letters
items.why: Ancient DNA has the same four letters as all DNA. The other three are the real difficulties.

items.p: Why do scientists who read ancient DNA wear suits, masks and gloves?
items.a: Their own skin, hair and breath carry human DNA. If it reached the bone powder, it would be read along with the ancient DNA and could be mistaken for it. The suit, mask and gloves keep it out.
items.why: A strong answer says that the danger is the scientist's own DNA, and that it looks very like the DNA being studied.

items.p: Put the steps of reading ancient DNA in order, from first to last.
a: Drill a little powder from inside the bone
Collect the short DNA pieces from the powder
Read the letters of each piece by machine
Line the pieces up where they overlap
Check each place against many pieces
items.why: The sample is taken first, then the pieces are read, then a computer puts them in order. Checking comes last, because one damaged piece could mislead.
items: Read the letters of each piece by machine
Check each place against many pieces
Drill a little powder from inside the bone
Line the pieces up where they overlap
Collect the short DNA pieces from the powder

items.p: True or false: people in Africa carry no Neanderthal DNA at all.
items.why: False. A 2020 study found a little, about 0.3 percent. It was probably carried back by people who returned to Africa.

items.p: Two children argue about Neanderthals.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, or says the question cannot be settled, and gives at least one piece of evidence. It also says what the other child has right.
items.why: Scientists themselves disagree. Kavya has the clear differences in the bones. Nila has the children born between the two groups. Both are using real evidence.

views.says: Neanderthals were a different species. Their skulls and bodies were clearly different from ours.
They were the same species as us. They had children with our ancestors.

items.ask: Whom do you agree with more? Give one piece of evidence. Then say one thing the other child has right.

items.p: Which finding first showed that Denisovans existed?
items.why: The DNA in a finger bone matched no known kind of human. No skull was linked to Denisovans until years later.

items.p: Label a drawing of two chromosomes crossing over.
a: Chromosome from the grandmother
Chromosome from the grandfather
The place where they cross
The new mixed chromosome
items.why: The new chromosome is part one grandparent's and part the other's. The crossing place is different every time.
items.art: Two long strips of different colours crossing in an X, and below them one strip that changes colour partway along, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Why can proteins sometimes identify a fossil when DNA cannot?
opts: DNA is found only in teeth
items.why: Proteins such as collagen break down more slowly than DNA. They do break down in the end, so 'never' is wrong.

worksheets.title: Evidence, Doubt and What Makes Us Human (challenge)

items.p: Scientists knew Denisovans existed before they had a skull. What could DNA tell them, and what could it not?
items.a: DNA could tell them that Denisovans were a separate group, who their nearest relatives were, and that they had children with Neanderthals and with our ancestors. It could not show their faces, their height, their tools or how they lived.
items.why: A strong answer gives at least one thing on each side.

items.p: In the paper test the red share kept halving. Why does the real Neanderthal share stay near 2 percent?
opts: The paper test was wrong in every way
items.why: In the paper test every partner was all white. In real life, after the mixing, most people in the group carried some pieces, so the average stopped falling quickly.

items.p: Three children argue about what makes our kind of human different.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view, or combines two, and gives evidence. It also names one thing that does not fit the view chosen.
items.why: Scientists hold all three views. Language helps teaching, but nobody knows whether Neanderthals spoke. Big groups keep ideas alive. And nearly every single ability has been found elsewhere.

views.says: Language. Words let us teach skills that are too hard to learn by watching.
Nothing single. Other humans and other animals do a little of everything we do.
Living in big groups that share ideas, so nothing useful is forgotten.

items.ask: Whom do you agree with most? Give one piece of evidence. Then name one fact that does not fit your view.

items.p: True or false: making tools is something only our species does.
items.why: False. Chimpanzees, crows and several earlier kinds of humans make tools.

items.p: Put these shares of DNA in order, from smallest to largest.
a: Neanderthal DNA in people in Africa
Neanderthal DNA in people outside Africa
Denisovan DNA in the Ayta Magbukon people
Neanderthal DNA in the man from Romania
Neanderthal DNA in Denny
items.why: The shares are about 0.3 percent, 2 percent, 5 percent, 6 to 9 percent and 50 percent. The closer in time to a Neanderthal ancestor, the larger the share.
items: Neanderthal DNA in people outside Africa
Neanderthal DNA in the man from Romania
Neanderthal DNA in people in Africa
Denisovan DNA in the Ayta Magbukon people

items.p: A new fossil jaw is found in India. Name three tests scientists could do, and what each could show.
items.a: They could study its shape, for example whether it has a chin, to judge the kind of human. They could date the layer it lay in to find its age. They could test its proteins, and look for DNA, to see who its relatives were.
items.why: A strong answer names shape, dating and proteins or DNA, and says that DNA may not have lasted in the heat.

items.p: Three of these are ideas about why Neanderthals disappeared. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Our ancestors came in larger numbers
items.why: Neanderthal brains were as large as ours. The other three are ideas that scientists take seriously.

items.p: A fossil's mitochondrial DNA is the Neanderthal kind. What does that prove, taken alone?
opts: Only that the mother's line was Neanderthal
That the father was a Neanderthal
That the fossil is our species
items.why: Mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother. Denny's was Neanderthal, yet her father was a Denisovan. The rest of the genome is needed for the father's side.

items.p: Draw the human family of the last 350,000 years as a bush. Show five kinds and two arrows for mixing.
items.a: Five or more branches side by side, most ending before the top. One arrow from Neanderthals to our branch and one from Denisovans to our branch, or one between Neanderthals and Denisovans.
items.why: A strong drawing shows branches that overlap in time, and arrows that cross between them.
items.art: A blank page with a time scale up the left side from 350,000 years ago to today.

items.p: When each generation adds to the skills it learned from the last, this is called ____ culture.
a: cumulative
items.why: Cumulative means building up. It is one leading idea about what helped our kind of human.

items.p: In the Teaching Test, one learner was taught with words. Name one thing words can pass on that watching cannot.
items.a: Words can say which detail matters, such as keeping the flap's top edge level, and why. They can warn about a mistake before it happens, and answer a question. A watcher sees the movement but not what is important about it.
items.why: A strong answer gives something that cannot be seen: what matters, why, or what to avoid.

items.p: Sort each statement: known, argued about, or not known.
items.why: Science keeps these three apart. A claim moves from one group to another only when new evidence arrives.
items: Our ancestors and Neanderthals had children
Neanderthals made the red marks in Spanish caves
Which kind of human made the Attirampakkam tools

items.p: True or false: one strange result is enough for a scientist to announce a discovery.
items.why: False. A strange result is usually a mistake, so it must be repeated and checked first. Denny's result was tested on six separate samples.

items.p: What is the leading explanation for the small size of Homo floresiensis?
opts: On islands with little food, small bodies do better
items.why: A small body needs less food, so over many generations island animals often become smaller. The skeleton had adult teeth and bones, so she was not a child.

items.p: Match each finding to what it shows.
items.why: Each finding is evidence for one conclusion. Saying which evidence supports which claim is the main skill here.
pairs: Healed injuries on a Neanderthal man
One copy of each kind at every marker
Only short Neanderthal pieces in people today
A chin on a fossil jaw
The jaw is from our species
Old tools with no bones nearby

quiz.p: Which statement about the human family is correct?
opts: Each kind turned into the next
Several kinds lived at the same time
quiz.why: Fossils show several kinds alive together. Humans and chimpanzees share an ancestor, and neither came from the other.

quiz.p: On which continent did Denisovans live?
quiz.why: Denisovan fossils come from Siberia, the Tibetan Plateau and eastern Asia. No other kind of human reached the Americas or Antarctica.

quiz.p: What can the teeth in a fossil jaw tell a scientist?
opts: About how old the person was
quiz.why: Teeth come through in a fixed order and have growth lines, so they show age. Words and names leave no trace in bone.

quiz.p: True or false: a fossil skull can show what a person thought about.
quiz.why: False. A skull shows the size and shape of the brain's space, not the thoughts. Thoughts leave no fossil.

quiz.p: What happens to DNA after a living being dies?
opts: It slowly breaks into short pieces
quiz.why: Repair stops at death, and water slowly cuts the DNA. After thousands of years the pieces are very short.

quiz.p: Where does most of the DNA in an old bone usually come from?
opts: Microbes that lived in the bone
quiz.why: Microbes move into a bone after death and leave their DNA. The person's own DNA is often a small part, which is why the work is hard.

quiz.p: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, what made the red piece shorter in each new row?
opts: Crossing over with a white chromosome
quiz.why: Each new row copied only one side from the row above. The other side came from a white partner, so part of the red was swapped away.

quiz.p: Two people each carry about 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. How do their pieces compare?
opts: They are exactly the same pieces
One of them must have none
Both have a whole Neanderthal chromosome
quiz.why: Chance decided which pieces each family line kept. That is why the pieces of many people together cover so much more of the genome.

quiz.p: Which evidence shows that our ancestors had children with Neanderthals?
opts: Neanderthal DNA pieces in living people
quiz.why: Tools and bones show that Neanderthals existed. Only shared DNA shows that children were born between the two groups.

quiz.p: A bone's DNA has one Neanderthal and one Denisovan copy all along every chromosome. What does that show?
opts: A mistake in the laboratory, always
quiz.why: Each parent gives one copy of every chromosome. Unbroken copies of two kinds mean the parents themselves were of the two kinds. A long-mixed family would show patches.

quiz.p: Which of these is found only in our species, as far as we know?
quiz.why: Neanderthals used fire, made tools and cared for injured friends. Writing is only about 5,000 years old.

quiz.p: Which of these is still not known?
opts: Which kind of human made India's oldest stone tools
Whether children get DNA from parents
Whether our species began in Africa
quiz.why: India's oldest tools have no bones with them and no DNA has lasted, so the makers are unknown. The other three are well supported by evidence.

applications: Doctors study the Neanderthal and Denisovan pieces in people's DNA. Some pieces change how the body fights infections, so they help explain why people respond differently to the same illness.
The 2025 study of 2,762 people in India mapped these old pieces along with newer changes. Maps like this help doctors look for the causes of diseases that are common in Indian families.
Police laboratories identify people from tiny, damaged traces of DNA. Many of their methods for short and damaged DNA were first worked out on ancient bones.
Clean rooms and blank samples, which you tried in The Clean Sample, are used wherever a tiny trace matters: in hospital test laboratories, in forensic laboratories and in making computer chips.
The collagen test that found Denny's bone is used by archaeologists to name thousands of bone scraps quickly. It shows which animals people hunted and herded.
Scientists who protect endangered animals read DNA from old museum skins and bones. It shows how much variety a species has lost.
Doctors who treat mountain sickness study the EPAS1 gene, which many Tibetan people got from Denisovans, to understand how a body copes with thin air.

open_questions.q: Why is our species the only kind of human left?
open_questions.why_open: Small numbers, changing climate, competition and mixing may all have played a part. The evidence cannot yet say how much each one mattered.

open_questions.q: Which kinds of humans lived in India before our species, and who made the oldest tools here?
open_questions.why_open: India has many very old stone tools and almost no old human bones. No ancient human DNA has lasted in the heat.

open_questions.q: Could Neanderthals and Denisovans speak as we do?
open_questions.why_open: Speech leaves no fossil. They had the same version of one speech gene, but many genes and much learning are needed for language.

open_questions.q: Where did the small island humans, Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis, come from?
open_questions.why_open: No DNA or protein has been recovered from them. From bones alone, scientists cannot agree which older humans were their ancestors.

open_questions.q: Do the few DNA changes that only people today share make any difference to how we think?
open_questions.why_open: The list of changes is known. What each change does in a growing brain is only beginning to be tested.

open_questions.q: Were there other kinds of humans whom nobody has found yet?
open_questions.why_open: The DNA of living people in Africa and Asia holds pieces that match no known fossil. Some scientists read these as traces of unknown groups.

maths.problem: In one family line of the Shrinking Pieces Test, the red squares in rows 1, 2 and 3 were 20, 8 and 3 out of 20. Write each as a fraction of the chromosome and as a percentage.
maths.answer: Row 1 is 20 out of 20, which is 100 percent. Row 2 is 8 out of 20, which is two fifths, or 40 percent. Row 3 is 3 out of 20, or 15 percent.
maths.explain: Each square is one twentieth of the chromosome, and one twentieth is 5 percent. So 8 squares are 8 × 5 = 40 percent, and 3 squares are 3 × 5 = 15 percent.
maths.context: This is about the Shrinking Pieces Test. There a row of 20 squares stands for one chromosome, and red squares are DNA from one ancestor.
maths.why_maths: Scientists report Neanderthal DNA as a percentage of the genome. A percentage lets you compare your paper lines with real people.

maths.problem: Suppose an ancestor's share of DNA exactly halved in every generation, starting from 100 percent. After how many halvings would it first fall below 2 percent? The mixing with Neanderthals was more than 1,500 generations ago. Why is the real share not close to zero?
maths.answer: After 6 halvings the share is about 1.6 percent, which is below 2 percent. The real share is not close to zero because the halving stopped once nearly everyone in the group carried some pieces.
maths.explain: 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, 3.125, 1.5625. That is 6 halvings. Halving happens only when the other parent has none of the ancestor's DNA. After a few generations of mixing, both parents carried pieces, so a child lost some and gained some.
maths.context: This is about the Shrinking Pieces Test. There the red share fell quickly because every partner was all white.
maths.why_maths: Following the halving pattern shows what the paper model predicts. Comparing that with the real 2 percent shows where the model is too simple.

maths.problem: A human genome has about 3 billion DNA letters. About 2 percent of the genome of a person outside Africa came from Neanderthals. About how many letters is that?
maths.explain: 1 percent of 3,000,000,000 is 30,000,000. So 2 percent is 2 × 30,000,000 = 60,000,000, which is 60 million. A small percentage of a very large number is still a large number.
maths.context: This is about the Shrinking Pieces Test, where one line might keep 1 square out of 20. In a real genome the pieces are counted in DNA letters.
maths.why_maths: The words '2 percent' sound tiny. Working out the number of letters shows how much DNA that really is.

maths.problem: On the Who Lived When time line, 1 centimetre is 10,000 years. The bar for our species is 31.5 centimetres long. The Neanderthal bar ends 4 centimetres from today. For how many years did both kinds live at the same time? About what fraction of our species' time is that?
maths.answer: 275,000 years. That is about seven eighths of our species' time.
maths.explain: 31.5 − 4 = 27.5 centimetres, and 27.5 × 10,000 = 275,000 years. As a fraction, 27.5 out of 31.5 is about 0.87, which is close to seven eighths. So we shared the Earth with Neanderthals for most of our history.
maths.context: This is about Who Lived When. There each kind of human is a bar on a time line of the last 350,000 years.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the bars and comparing the lengths turns 'a long time' into a share you can picture.

maths.problem: Most of the mixing between our ancestors and Neanderthals happened about 47,000 years ago. If one generation is about 25 years, how many generations ago was that? In the Shrinking Pieces Test you did 4 generations of crossing over. How many times more is the real number?
maths.answer: About 1,880 generations ago. That is 470 times as many as in the test.
maths.explain: 47,000 ÷ 25 = 1,880. Then 1,880 ÷ 4 = 470. After so many rounds of crossing over, the Neanderthal pieces in people today are very short.
maths.context: This is about the Shrinking Pieces Test. There each new row was one generation, and crossing over cut the red piece once in each row.
maths.why_maths: Dividing years by the length of a generation tells you how many times the DNA has been cut. That explains why the real pieces are so short.

maths.problem: In row 5 of the Shrinking Pieces Test, line A kept squares 3, 4 and 5. Line E kept squares 12 and 13. The other four lines kept nothing. What fraction of the chromosome is red in the All Together row? Could the All Together row ever have less red than the best single line?
maths.answer: 5 out of 20, which is one quarter. No, the All Together row can never have less red than the best single line.
maths.explain: 3 + 2 = 5 squares, because the two pieces do not overlap, and 5 out of 20 is one quarter. Every red square in any line is also red in the All Together row. So it has at least as much red as the best line, and more whenever the pieces sit in different places.
maths.context: This is about the Shrinking Pieces Test. There the All Together row is red wherever any of the six lines is red in row 5.
maths.why_maths: This is the reasoning scientists use when they join the pieces from thousands of people to rebuild part of a Neanderthal genome.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that our ancestors and Neanderthals had children together? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1997, Matthias Krings and Svante Pääbo read the first Neanderthal DNA. It came from the arm bone of the first Neanderthal ever recognised, found in Germany in 1856. They could read only a small piece of mitochondrial DNA, the loop that passes from mother to child. It was unlike the mitochondrial DNA of any living person. Many scientists concluded that Neanderthals had died out without leaving descendants. But mitochondrial DNA is a tiny part of a genome, and a family loses it whenever a mother has no daughters. So Pääbo's team spent years learning to read the whole genome from old bones. Most of the DNA in the bones came from microbes, and the human pieces were short and damaged. In 2010, Richard Green and the team published a first rough Neanderthal genome, read mostly from three bones from Vindija Cave in Croatia. People outside Africa shared more of it than people in Africa south of the Sahara did. Neanderthals and our ancestors had mixed. Pääbo received a Nobel Prize in 2022.
how_we_found_out.who: Matthias Krings, Svante Pääbo, Richard Green and their team at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig, Germany
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That Neanderthals died out without leaving any descendants. Reading the whole genome showed that people outside Africa carry between 1 and 4 percent Neanderthal DNA. Later work put the figure at about 2 percent.
how_we_found_out.art: Three brown thigh bone pieces on a clean tray, with a long printed ribbon of DNA letters running from them to a map where Europe and Asia glow faintly.

roots.context: We have learned that several kinds of humans once lived together, and that some of their DNA is still in living people. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, most family lines lost every red square, yet different lines kept different red pieces. Neanderthals ended as a separate people about 40,000 years ago. But most people alive carry small pieces of their DNA, and together the pieces make up about half a Neanderthal genome. So a kind of human can end as a group and still go on, in pieces, inside another.
deep_truth.habit: We use the word 'extinct' to mean completely gone, and we speak of 'them' and 'us' as two separate peoples. The DNA shows that the Neanderthals' ending and our own history overlap. Some Neanderthals were among our ancestors' mothers and fathers.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Shrinking Pieces Test, no single line kept much red, but the lines together kept more. In 2010 the Neanderthal genome showed that people outside Africa carry Neanderthal pieces. In 2025, scientists joined the pieces carried by 2,762 people in India and recovered about half of a Neanderthal genome.

three.who_am_i: You are Homo sapiens, and you are also a little more than that. If your ancestors lived outside Africa, about 2 percent of your DNA came from Neanderthals, and a trace came from Denisovans.
three.what_is_life: Life does not keep its kinds in sealed boxes. Two groups drift apart slowly, and for a very long time they can still meet and become one family again.
three.what_is_this_world: For most of our species' time, the world held several kinds of humans at once. A world with only one kind of human is new and unusual.

roots.thread: Every kind of human came from one earlier people in Africa. That one people became many: Neanderthals in the west, Denisovans in the east, small humans on islands, and our own ancestors in Africa. Each kind met the world with their own bodies and their own minds, and each of them thought, felt and decided. Then some of the many met, and their children joined them into one family again. Both the parting and the joining are written in your cells.

science.text: All living people share ancestors who lived in Africa within the last 300,000 years.
People outside Africa carry about 2 percent Neanderthal DNA, and some peoples carry up to 5 percent Denisovan DNA.
Whether Neanderthals were a separate species or a group within our own is still argued.
Whether any single change made our kind of human different from the others is not known.

other_view.who: Many scientists who study fossil bones, such as Ian Tattersall
other_view.view: Neanderthals were a separate species, and they truly became extinct. A few scattered pieces of DNA are not a people. Their bodies, their way of life and their own line of families ended about 40,000 years ago. Saying that they live on in us hides a real loss.

practice.title: The line behind you
practice.say: Sit still and touch your chin. Only our kind of human has a chin like this. Now put your hand on your chest and breathe slowly five times. On each breath, think of one mother further back: your mother, her mother, and so on. The line does not stop after five. It goes back without a break to people who were not our kind of human. Sit quietly for a moment with that line behind you.
practice.kid: Touch your chin. Only our kind of human has one. Now breathe slowly five times. On each breath, think of one mother further back. The line goes on and never breaks. Sit quietly and feel that long line behind you.

ask: If part of a people lives on inside another people, is that people gone?
Where would you draw the line between 'us' and 'them', and what would you use to draw it?
Is being the only kind of human left something to be proud of, sad about, or neither?
What can you never know about Denny, however good the science becomes?

playtest: What was checked. The Shrinking Pieces Test was run 20,000 times on a computer with the same rules as the paper version: 20 squares, one cut from a chit numbered 1 to 19, a coin for the side, four rounds of crossing over. On average about 30 in 100 lines still have red in row 5, so one, two or three lines of six is usual, and all six lines are white about one time in eight. The step tells you what to do then. The time line in Who Lived When was checked by counting the bars at 30, 10 and 2 centimetres. The marker rows in Whose Child were checked letter by letter. Facts, dates and names were checked by web search on 19 November 2026 against Wikipedia pages and the journal or press pages for the main papers: Denny and the 2,315 bone pieces, the Denisovan fossils, the shares of Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA, the 47,000 year date, the 2025 study in India, the Narmada skull, Shanidar, Homo naledi, Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis, Jebel Irhoud, Ngandong and the 2015 teaching experiment. What a parent should know. The paper cup fold was written from the standard fold and not folded here: fold one yourself first. The Teaching Test needs two or three learners and gives a small result, so treat it as a first look. In Warm or Cold the fizz times were not measured here. Warm water should finish clearly first, and the step says what to do if all three are too quick to time. The YouTube addresses, titles and channels of the three videos were confirmed, but the videos were not watched: please preview them. Journal volume and page numbers in the sources list were not all checked one by one.

did_you_know.text: Robert Bruce Foote found the first stone hand axe in India at Pallavaram in 1863. You can see stone hand axes at the Government Museum in Egmore, Chennai.
Near Chennai, at Attirampakkam, people made hand axes about 1.5 million years ago. No bones were found, so nobody knows which kind of human they were.
